paragraphs: A tensor ring decomposition represents a multidimensional data array using a collection of smaller components called cores. Computing those cores can become expensive when the original array contains many entries. This paper proposes fitting the representation through carefully selected samples, reducing the amount of data involved in the repeated fitting calculations.

The method uses alternating least squares: it iteratively updates the cores through least squares problems. Its sampling strategy relies on leverage scores, which guide which parts of those problems to retain. By exploiting the structure of tensor rings, the authors estimate these scores efficiently and obtain computational complexity that is sublinear in the number of input entries.

The theoretical guarantees concern the sampled least squares problems: their relative errors are controlled with high probability. Experiments on synthetic and real data show substantial speed improvements while preserving good accuracy, with some speedups reaching two or three orders of magnitude. A feature extraction example also illustrates how the faster decomposition can support another data processing task.
icml-2021-a-sampling-based-method-for-te.tldr: Sampling guided by efficiently estimated leverage scores speeds up tensor ring decomposition while retaining good empirical accuracy.

paragraphs: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis often compresses gene measurements into a latent representation, groups cells there, and then selects genes to explain the groups. Treating these as separate steps can disconnect the explanation from how the groups were formed. In particular, nonlinear transformations and relationships among genes can affect which genes actually distinguish the resulting clusters.

ACE combines representation learning, clustering, and explanation within one deep learning workflow. Its output is a panel of explanatory genes, broadening the usual emphasis on marker genes. A useful panel can include genes expressed more strongly or less strongly than in other cell types, as well as genes that separate closely related types.

The experiments show that ACE can identify panels that distinguish clusters well without excessive redundancy among their genes. This matters because an explanation should capture complementary differences, rather than repeatedly describe the same distinction. The authors also demonstrate the framework on image recognition, showing an application beyond the gene expression setting that motivates the work.
icml-2021-ace-explaining-cluster-from-an.tldr: ACE jointly learns cell representations, clusters, and explanatory gene panels that empirically distinguish cell types with little redundancy.

paragraphs: Engineering design often involves competing goals, uncertain performance measurements, and limits on how precisely a design can be built. Methods that search for the best tradeoffs usually emphasize objective values. That emphasis can leave a designer with little guidance about the range of actual configurations that would meet practical needs.

This paper changes the search target by asking for minimum acceptable performance on every objective. Those thresholds define a region of satisfaction in the space of design parameters. The task becomes finding configurations throughout that acceptable region, making the variety and location of workable designs part of the search itself.

The proposed Expected Coverage Improvement algorithm actively selects evaluations to discover this region efficiently while also sampling diverse acceptable configurations. The authors demonstrate it in mechanical design, additive manufacturing, medical monitoring, and plasma physics. The contribution is a formulation and search method that connect performance requirements to choices in parameter space, addressing the practical importance of uncertainty and implementation precision.
icml-2021-beyond-the-pareto-efficient-fr.tldr: Expected Coverage Improvement searches for diverse designs that meet all performance thresholds, making acceptable regions in parameter space the goal.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether a model trained in some environments can work in unseen ones. A common approach makes representations independent of the environment after accounting for the class label. This paper provides counterexamples showing that satisfying this condition alone does not ensure generalization, because important differences can remain among objects within the same class.

The authors use a structural causal model to distinguish an object's causal features from non-causal features changed by the domain. Their alternative objective matches representations of observations derived from the same underlying object across domains. They develop matching algorithms for observed object correspondences and MatchDG to approximate this objective when those correspondences are unavailable.

The algorithms achieve competitive out-of-domain accuracy on rotated MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, PACS, and Chest-Xray data. MatchDG also recovers meaningful object correspondences: its top ten matches overlap ground-truth matches by more than half on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. These findings support matching within classes as a useful training objective, while the counterexamples establish why class-level invariance alone can be inadequate.
icml-2021-domain-generalization-using-ca.tldr: Matching the same underlying objects across domains addresses a weakness of class-conditional invariance and yields competitive generalization results.

paragraphs: Predicting who may become infected could help identify candidates for preventive intervention. Training such models is difficult when testing is limited and favors people with symptoms. The observed records then give an incomplete and biased picture of infection, since some infected people may carry the disease without being tested.

The paper investigates whether useful prediction remains possible under this testing process. Its analysis suggests that incomplete testing might still support good predictions on new data when infection is highly transmissible. Guided by that conditional finding, the authors develop an infection prediction algorithm and show that it outperforms comparison methods on simulated data.

The authors also apply the model to hospital data on Clostridioides difficile, which includes symptomatic infections and asymptomatic carriers. Because the infection status of untested people is unobserved, this evaluation uses a proxy for that state. The model outperforms benchmarks in this setting, providing empirical support for the approach while preserving the distinction between proxy-based evaluation and directly observing every infection.
icml-2021-exploiting-structured-data-for.tldr: The paper develops an infection predictor motivated by evidence that highly transmissible diseases may remain predictable despite incomplete, symptom-biased testing.

paragraphs: Generating a molecule as a graph requires choosing discrete nodes and edges. The paper argues that using continuous latent variables for this task can model those discrete structures inaccurately. GraphDF addresses that mismatch by keeping its latent representation discrete, aligning the variables used for generation with the kind of objects being generated.

The model builds on normalizing flows and uses invertible modulo shift transformations to turn discrete latent variables into graph nodes and edges. Invertibility means these transformations can be reversed. This construction gives GraphDF a way to generate graph structures without relying on the continuous conversion associated with dequantization.

The authors report that discrete latent variables reduce computational costs and remove the negative effect of dequantization. Their experiments find that GraphDF outperforms prior methods in random molecular generation, property optimization, and constrained optimization. Together, these results support the paper's central design choice: directly modeling discrete structure can improve both computational efficiency and empirical performance across several molecular generation tasks.
icml-2021-graphdf-a-discrete-flow-model-.tldr: GraphDF uses invertible transformations of discrete latent variables to generate molecular graphs, reducing computation and improving results across three generation tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies designing small antennas and antenna arrays to produce a requested radiation pattern. The designs must also fit specified dimensions and include predetermined locations in their metallic structure. These requirements make the task more specific than simply finding a shape with desirable radiation behavior: the result must satisfy physical layout conditions too.

For a single antenna, the authors combine a simulation network, a hypernetwork, and a refinement network. For an array, they introduce another design level by placing a hypernetwork within a hypernetwork. Training evaluates how closely the resulting radiation pattern matches the requested pattern, connecting the learned design process to the desired electromagnetic behavior.

Experiments show that the approach generates new antennas and arrays satisfying the requirements and performs considerably better than the tested baselines. Comparisons also reveal substantial overlap with existing designs. In a cellular phone antenna array example, the generated solution improves on properties of the existing design, illustrating the method's potential for a concrete constrained design problem.
icml-2021-hyperhypernetwork-for-the-desi.tldr: Nested hypernetworks generate antennas and antenna arrays that meet layout requirements while matching requested radiation patterns.

paragraphs: Learning graph patterns that span longer paths requires deeper graph neural networks in the setting studied here. Yet increasing depth often reduces performance. The paper examines graphs with edge features and argues that common approaches to this problem address only part of how training signals travel through the network.

Normalization and skip connections often help signals pass between successive representations of the same node. The authors distinguish this depth-wise flow from breadth-wise flow between neighboring nodes. They construct synthetic datasets to examine long-range learning and propose an attention-based architecture designed to improve backpropagation along both kinds of connections.

On these testbeds, several common architectures with only depth-wise skip connections struggle to learn long-range patterns. The proposed architecture clearly outperforms them, and the authors also find it competitive on real-world data. These results make the distinction between the two directions consequential: improving connections through layers alone did not provide the same long-range learning performance in the reported tests.
icml-2021-improving-breadth-wise-backpro.tldr: An attention-based graph network improves training signals across both layers and neighboring nodes, helping it learn long-range patterns.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents may need to respect practical restrictions that are difficult to write down mathematically. This paper studies learning those restrictions from demonstrations by an agent that already follows them. The objective is to infer the constraints behind the observed behavior, making them available to guide other agents.

The framework learns in a model-free setting, so it does not assume knowledge of the environment's transition dynamics. It supports high-dimensional problems and arbitrary Markovian constraints within that setting. This broadens the scope beyond earlier approaches described as relying on discrete environments, particular constraint types, or known transition dynamics.

Experiments show that the approach can recover the most likely constraints respected by the demonstrator. The learned constraints also transfer to agents with different morphologies, reward functions, or both. That transfer is central to the contribution: restrictions inferred from one agent's behavior can remain useful when another agent pursues a different objective or has a different physical form.
icml-2021-inverse-constrained-reinforcem.tldr: The framework learns Markovian constraints from compliant demonstrations and experimentally transfers them to agents with different bodies or rewards.

paragraphs: Reliable wireless communication depends on encoding information so that a decoder can recover it after noise corrupts transmission. This paper introduces KO codes, a family of learned encoder and decoder pairs. Their goal is to improve reliability while retaining computational efficiency, with evaluation on the standard additive white Gaussian noise channel.

The neural architectures are inspired by the computation tree of the Kronecker operation used in Reed-Muller and Polar codes. The authors attribute the gains primarily to a nonlinear mapping from information bits directly to transmitted symbols, bypassing a separate modulation step. The architecture also provides an efficient decoder, making decoding performance part of the design.

In the short-to-medium block length regime, KO codes outperform the compared Reed-Muller and Polar codes using low-complexity successive cancellation decoding on that channel. This is a result within the stated channel and decoding comparison. More broadly, the construction points toward exploring richer nonlinear coding structures while preserving an efficient way to recover the transmitted information.
icml-2021-ko-codes-inventing-nonlinear-e.tldr: KO codes learn efficient nonlinear encoders and decoders that improve reliability over the stated Reed-Muller and Polar comparisons on the AWGN channel.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer interaction rules from trajectories of agents whose motion is constrained to a curved geometric space. These rules, called interaction kernels, describe how agents influence one another. Accounting for the geometry matters because both the distance between agents and the direction of their interaction are defined on the manifold.

The models assume that interactions depend on pairwise Riemannian distances and act locally along the shortest geodesic connecting the agents. Within this model class, the authors construct estimators and prove a convergence rate independent of the dimension of the state space. They also bound the discrepancy between trajectories produced by the estimated and observed dynamics.

The estimator is demonstrated on opinion dynamics and a predator-swarm system, each placed on a sphere and on the Poincaré disk representation of hyperbolic space. The contribution combines geometry-aware learning with theoretical control of both interaction estimation and trajectory error. Its dimension-independent rate concerns the specified interaction model rather than every possible dynamical system on a manifold.
icml-2021-learning-interaction-kernels-f.tldr: The paper learns distance-based interaction rules on manifolds with dimension-independent convergence rates and bounds on trajectory estimation error.

paragraphs: Learning how a population changes is harder when observations do not follow the same individuals over time. An individual seen at one time may be absent later, or identities may be unavailable entirely. The paper addresses learning nonlinear stochastic dynamics from these aggregate observations, where complete individual trajectories cannot serve as training data.

The method describes the evolution of the population's density through a sampled version of the weak form of the Fokker Planck equation. It combines this description with a Wasserstein generative adversarial network during training. This provides a way to connect observations across time through their distributions, without requiring identities to link individual measurements.

A central computational feature is that learning does not require explicitly solving the Fokker Planck partial differential equation. The authors demonstrate the approach on synthetic and real-world datasets. The work therefore offers a sample-based route to learning dynamics in a data setting that differs fundamentally from the complete-trajectory setting assumed by many existing methods.
icml-2021-learning-stochastic-behaviour-.tldr: A sampled weak-form Fokker Planck model combined with a WGAN learns nonlinear stochastic dynamics without complete individual trajectories.

paragraphs: A model trained to resist one category of adversarial perturbation can still face other kinds of attacks. Training against several categories at once can also substantially increase computational cost. This paper addresses both issues with a meta-learning framework that learns how to generate training noise useful for robustness across multiple perturbation types.

Its central component, the Meta Noise Generator, produces noise that randomly perturbs a given sample. The generator is trained so that these perturbed samples help reduce error under diverse adversarial perturbations. The prediction model then learns from the generated samples while being encouraged to keep its labels consistent across multiple perturbations.

The authors evaluate models trained this way on several datasets and a wide variety of perturbations. They report significant improvements over the tested baselines across multiple perturbations, with only marginal computational cost. The findings support learning a noise generator as a practical training mechanism for broader attack coverage, with the reported robustness established by those experimental evaluations.
icml-2021-learning-to-generate-noise-for.tldr: A meta-learned noise generator improves empirical robustness to multiple attack types with marginal computational cost.

paragraphs: Local graph clustering helps analyze large networks by finding relevant groups of vertices. Many methods seek a single group with relatively few connections leading outside it, an objective described by low conductance. This paper instead focuses on the connections between groups, making the relationship between two sets part of what the algorithm seeks.

The authors study local algorithms that find a pair of vertex sets according to their interconnection and their links to the rest of the graph. Their main analytical tool is a reduction that transforms questions about multiple sets into a question about one set in a modified graph. This connects the paired structure to a simpler form of graph analysis.

The algorithms successfully recover densely connected clusters in the Interstate Disputes Dataset and the US Migration Dataset. These applications illustrate the value of examining groups through their mutual relationships. The contribution expands the clustering target from the isolation of one group to the joint structure of two groups and their surrounding network.
icml-2021-local-algorithms-for-finding-d.tldr: New local graph algorithms find pairs of densely connected clusters by reducing a multiple-set structure to a single-set problem.

paragraphs: A classifier's probability estimates should communicate how reliable its predictions are, alongside the predictions themselves. Many classifiers, especially deep neural networks, produce probabilities that are poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration addresses this by learning a mapping that adjusts a trained model's probability outputs, but the paper argues that low calibration error alone is an inadequate design goal.

The authors introduce two additional constraints for constructing a useful calibration map. Meta-Cal combines a base calibrator with a ranking model to address this broader formulation. Under assumptions described as mild, they establish two high-probability bounds concerning the constraints, giving theoretical control beyond simply minimizing an observed calibration error.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with a range of popular network architectures. The authors report that Meta-Cal significantly outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods for post-hoc multiclass calibration. The work pairs empirical improvement with conditional guarantees, emphasizing that the usefulness of adjusted probabilities depends on more than one calibration quality criterion.
icml-2021-meta-cal-well-controlled-post-.tldr: Meta-Cal combines calibration and ranking to improve multiclass probability estimates while providing conditional bounds for two additional calibration constraints.

paragraphs: The paper studies clustering whose assignments can be explained by a threshold decision tree. Each internal node tests one feature and splits the data into two groups, while the full tree produces k clusters. The challenge is to retain this readable decision structure while keeping the k-medians or k-means clustering objective small.

The proposed algorithm improves competitive guarantees from O(k) to approximately logarithmic in k for k-medians with the l1 norm, and from O(k²) to approximately linear in k for k-means. These approximate descriptions suppress the factors hidden by the paper's tilde notation. A separate algorithm achieves an O((log k)^(3/2)) guarantee for k-medians with the l2 norm.

Lower bounds clarify how much further these guarantees can improve. Together with an existing logarithmic lower bound for l1 k-medians, the paper's new approximately linear lower bound for k-means makes the first algorithm near-optimal. It also proves a logarithmic lower bound for l2 k-medians. The results quantify the clustering-cost tradeoff imposed by requiring simple, feature-by-feature explanations.
icml-2021-near-optimal-algorithms-for-ex.tldr: New decision-tree clustering algorithms improve approximation guarantees, with lower bounds establishing near-optimality for l1 k-medians and k-means.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a continuous surface from a collection of 3D points requires a representation that fills in the geometry between observations. Neural-Pull learns a signed distance function with a neural network. Its training task is to move query locations toward their closest surface points using quantities that the network itself predicts.

For each query location, the predicted distance determines how far to move, while the function's gradient provides the direction. The sign of the distance determines whether movement follows or opposes that gradient. Because the pulling operation is differentiable, training can update the predicted distance and the gradient together through the same operation.

This connects learning the surface representation to the geometric action of pulling space onto the surface. On widely used benchmarks, the authors report more accurate and flexible signed distance learning than the compared state-of-the-art methods for surface reconstruction and single-image reconstruction. The stated results support using the predicted function and its gradient jointly as the basis of reconstruction training.
icml-2021-neural-pull-learning-signed-di.tldr: Neural-Pull learns surface distance functions by differentiably moving 3D queries toward the surface using predicted distances and gradients.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs describe generative models and rely on inference engines to compute posterior distributions. Programs with random branching or recursion can define models whose parameter space is infinite-dimensional. This creates a mismatch with standard Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which is designed to target distributions with a fixed number of parameters.

The paper introduces Nonparametric Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to extend HMC to this broader model setting. Its inputs are a newly defined class of measurable functions called tree representable functions. These provide a representation of probabilistic program densities that does not depend on a particular programming language, separating the inference method from the syntax used to express a model.

The authors prove the algorithm's correctness and report significant performance gains over existing approaches on several nonparametric examples. The contribution therefore addresses both the formal validity and the practical promise of extending HMC beyond fixed-dimensional models. It advances the stated goal of general-purpose inference for expressive probabilistic programs through a specific representation and accompanying algorithm.
icml-2021-nonparametric-hamiltonian-mont.tldr: NP-HMC extends Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to nonparametric probabilistic programs using tree representable densities, with a correctness proof and empirical gains.

paragraphs: After a neural network is trained with stochastic gradient descent, moving its parameters along a straight line from their initial values to their final values often steadily lowers the training objective. This monotonic linear interpolation property is striking because the objective is nonconvex and the actual training process can follow highly nonlinear dynamics.

The paper investigates explanations for this observation using differential geometry. It relates the straight path in parameter space to the corresponding path of network functions. For mean squared error, the authors provide sufficient conditions for monotonicity. These conditions establish circumstances in which the property holds, without claiming that every monotonic interpolation must satisfy them.

The study also shows that the property can be systematically violated in practice by encouraging weights to travel far from initialization. Although monotonic interpolation appears across multiple architectures and learning problems, it is therefore not universal. The combination of sufficient conditions and constructed violations helps sharpen questions about the global geometry of neural network training objectives.
icml-2021-on-monotonic-linear-interpolat.tldr: The paper gives sufficient geometric conditions for monotonic loss along parameter interpolation and systematically produces networks that violate the property.

paragraphs: The paper compares learning a differentiable model through gradient descent with learning through its associated tangent kernel. The central question is how much learning power the full differentiable model can have beyond the kernel approach. The analysis distinguishes accurate prediction from weak learning, which means obtaining any nontrivial advantage over random guessing.

Under certain conditions, the authors show that gradient descent can attain small error only if a related tangent kernel method can weakly learn. This is a necessary implication within those conditions, rather than an equivalence in predictive performance. The kernel's advantage can be very small even when gradient descent reaches arbitrarily high accuracy.

The complementary result removes those conditions and shows a stronger separation: gradient descent can learn with small error even when no kernel method obtains a nontrivial advantage over random guessing. Together, the results identify both a conditional connection and a possible gap between the approaches. A weak kernel signal can accompany highly accurate differentiable learning, but that connection does not hold without the stated conditions.
icml-2021-quantifying-the-benefit-of-usi.tldr: Gradient descent can greatly outperform tangent kernels, with even the existence of a weak kernel advantage depending on the theoretical conditions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning works empirically in complex nonlinear environments, but many sample-efficiency guarantees assume a linear structure in transitions or value functions. This paper seeks a different theoretical basis for learning in continuous state spaces. It introduces the Effective Planning Window condition, a structural requirement on the decision process that makes no linearity assumption.

The authors provide an algorithm that provably learns efficiently in environments satisfying this condition. Its assumptions on the policy class are minimal and permit multilayer neural networks with nonlinear activation functions. The condition is motivated directly by gaming benchmarks, and the paper shows that many classic Atari games satisfy it.

The analysis also establishes why dropping linearity does not eliminate the need for structural assumptions. The authors exhibit simple decision processes with slight nonlinearities that cannot be solved sample efficiently. These examples support the need for conditions like Effective Planning Window, while the positive result supplies one route to guarantees beyond linear models without asserting that this particular condition is universally necessary.
icml-2021-sample-efficient-reinforcement.tldr: The Effective Planning Window condition enables provably sample-efficient reinforcement learning without assuming linear transitions or value functions.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient methods can become unstable when gradients are unbounded or lack Lipschitz continuity. Gradient clipping limits unusually large updates and is widely used to stabilize training, but its convergence behavior is less well understood. This paper develops theoretical results for clipped stochastic gradient and subgradient methods in settings where standard regularity properties can fail.

For nonsmooth convex functions with rapidly growing subgradients, the authors establish both qualitative convergence results and quantitative rates. Their analysis shows improved stability from clipping and finite convergence rates in many cases. This places a commonly used practical technique on a firmer theoretical footing for the specified class of optimization problems.

The paper also analyzes a clipped momentum method, including clipped SGD as a special case, for weakly convex problems under standard assumptions. A new Lyapunov analysis yields the best-known rate for that problem class. Numerical results support the theoretical developments, connecting the stability motivation to convergence evidence across these two analyzed optimization regimes.
icml-2021-stability-and-convergence-of-s.tldr: The paper proves stability and convergence results for clipped stochastic optimization, including a best-known rate for the analyzed weakly convex setting.

paragraphs: In cooperative reinforcement learning, the number of joint action combinations grows exponentially with the number of agents. This makes action values difficult to represent accurately and can undermine the critic used by policy-gradient methods. Tesseract addresses this shared problem by seeking a compact representation that still captures interactions relevant to the task.

The paper reformulates the Bellman equation using tensors. It views the action-value function as a multidimensional array with one dimension corresponding to each agent's action space. Algorithms derived from this formulation decompose that array across agents and use low-rank approximations to represent their interactions with a lower-complexity model.

The authors connect accurate representation within a low-complexity hypothesis class to learning efficiency and provide a probably approximately correct analysis for Tesseract-based algorithms. They also discuss relevance to decision processes with rich observations. Experiments across different domains confirm gains in sample efficiency consistent with the theory, supporting tensor decomposition as a way to manage joint action complexity while modeling inter-agent dependencies.
icml-2021-tesseract-tensorised-actors-fo.tldr: Tesseract represents joint action values with low-rank tensors to model agent interactions compactly and improve sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Zero-shot coordination requires agents to collaborate with partners they did not encounter during training. Self-play can prepare an agent for a narrow range of situations because its own strategy shapes the trajectories it experiences. A new partner can create unfamiliar situations, making successful self-play a poor predictor of successful collaboration.

The paper trains a common best response against a population whose policies are explicitly encouraged to be diverse. Its Trajectory Diversity objective, or TrajeDi, is differentiable and generalizes the Jensen-Shannon divergence between policies. The approach makes diversity part of population training so that the responding agent faces a broader collection of behaviors.

The authors motivate the objective experimentally in two simple settings and then evaluate its scalability in the cooperative card game Hanabi. It improves cross-play scores over independently trained self-play agents and best responses to populations without diversity regularization. These results support deliberately shaping the training population as a means of improving coordination with previously unseen partners.
icml-2021-trajectory-diversity-for-zero-.tldr: TrajeDi encourages diverse training partners and improves zero-shot coordination in Hanabi by training a common response to that population.

paragraphs: Classical value iteration requires discretization when applied to continuous states and actions, which can make computation grow exponentially. This paper introduces continuous fitted value iteration, or cFVI, to extend dynamic programming to continuous environments. The method assumes a known dynamics model, making that model an explicit part of the learning setup.

The authors use a continuous-time formulation to derive the optimal policy in closed form for nonlinear control-affine dynamics. This analytical policy solution enables an efficient extension of value iteration without the same discretization burden. The stated dynamics structure is therefore central to how the method obtains its computational advantage.

In nonlinear control experiments, cFVI matches the quantitative performance of deep reinforcement learning methods in simulation and performs better when transferred to a physical system. Its learned policy also shows greater robustness to changes in dynamics. These are experimental findings despite using only a deterministic model and including no explicit robustness term in the optimization, highlighting a useful property of the tested solutions.
icml-2021-value-iteration-in-continuous-.tldr: cFVI uses known control-affine dynamics and a continuous-time policy solution to extend value iteration, with strong physical-transfer results in the reported experiments.
